payload.source_label: Equation (1.7): differentiating (1.5) and eliminating mixed derivatives gives p_tt = c^2 p_xx

contract.statement: For the one-dimensional constant-coefficient acoustic system p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0, with p the pressure perturbation, u the particle velocity, and c = √(K/ρ) the sound speed, the pressure satisfies p_tt = c² p_xx [printed page 2, equation (1.5) and definitions; printed page 3, equation (1.7)]. The source derives this by differentiating the first acoustic equation in time and the second in space and eliminating mixed derivatives of velocity, implicitly requiring sufficient regularity [printed page 3, paragraph after (1.7)]. It also calls the resulting second-order equation hyperbolic; exact regularity and parameter inequalities are left implicit in the physical context [printed pages 2–3, material definitions and classification paragraph after (1.7)].
assumptions: The pressure and velocity satisfy p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0 [printed page 2, equation (1.5); printed page 3, statement that (1.7) is obtained from (1.5)].
K and ρ are constant with respect to space and time [printed page 2, material described by the constants K and ρ].

The differentiation argument implicitly requires the relevant second derivatives and equality of the two orders of mixed differentiation of u; a precise regularity class is not stated [printed page 3, differentiation and mixed-derivative elimination explanation after (1.7)].

Use of 1/ρ and of the real sound speed √(K/ρ) presupposes meaningful coefficients in the intended physical setting; explicit inequalities on K and ρ are not listed in the selected surrounding passage [printed page 2, equation (1.5) and definition c = √(K/ρ)].
The application is simple acoustic waves propagating in both directions along a one-dimensional medium [printed page 2, introduction to (1.5); printed page 3, introduction to (1.7)].

The result concerns classical differentiation of the acoustic equations; the selected passage does not introduce a weak or distributional interpretation [printed page 3, differentiation explanation after (1.7)].

The source presents a forward derivation of a second-order pressure equation from the first-order system, without asserting a converse reconstruction of velocity [printed page 3, paragraph after (1.7)].
No initial or boundary conditions accompany this derivation [printed page 2, equation (1.5); printed page 3, equation (1.7) and its explanatory paragraph].
quantifiers: Spatial coordinate x and time coordinate t are real variables in the enclosing one-dimensional PDE framework; equation (1.7) suppresses their arguments [printed page 1, equation (1.1) and q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ^m; printed page 3, equation (1.7)].
p(x,t) and u(x,t) are scalar pressure and particle-velocity fields, respectively [printed page 2, equation (1.5) and following definitions].
K and ρ are constant material parameters; c is the sound speed defined by c = √(K/ρ), rather than an independent coefficient [printed page 2, definitions following (1.5) and (1.6)].

The displayed PDEs are understood at points where the fields and required derivatives are defined; no explicit quantified theorem or separate solution domain is supplied [printed pages 2–3, equations (1.5) and (1.7)].
